body_markdown:
It was a good year for the auctions at Monterey Car Week. Records were broken left and right;[total sales topped $756M](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/2026-monterey-car-week-auctions-shatter-record-with-756m-in-sales/) (!), and the *average* sale price was $885,765. A different world than the one most car fans live in, then, but even among these numbers with lots of commas, there *were* deals to be had and interesting vehicles hammered sold for less-than-stratospheric values.


We took a look at what you could have gotten at Monterey for $100K—still significantly more than most will spend on a car, but much more within the realm of possibility than the Shelby Daytona Coupe or the myriad Ferrari F50s sold there. Turns out 310 lots sold for a hundred grand or less, so there were plenty of good options to choose from. Here’s what our staff would have brought home with a hypothetical $100K—some of us “spent” quite a bit less.


## Hot Model A


Gooding Christie's


[This 1929 Model A hot rod](https://www.goodingco.com/lot/1929-ford-model-a-hot-rod) was my favorite car of all the auctions I attended at Monterey. It is a lovely preserved car that was hot-rodded in the late 1930s. The car had a bunch of trick speed parts from back in the era and was raced through the early 1950s. Few cars in Monterey oozed this much character, and I couldn’t help but be drawn to it every time I entered the Gooding Christie’s tent. Gooding mentioned that the car needed some mechanical attention after having been a static display. Since the car sold for $92,400, that leaves plenty of money to go over the mechanicals. — *Greg Ingold*


## Slippery Lotus


Mecum


The Lotus Eleven is one of my favorite cars from one of my favorite carmakers. It looks like a spaceship, weighs about 1000 pounds, and won a ton of races. It’s also worth a fraction of many of the cars it beat in period. Even by Eleven standards, though,[$66K for the one in Monterey](https://mecum.com/lots/1175021/1956-lotus-eleven-le-man) seems very cheap. Maybe Mecum was a weird venue for it, or maybe there’s something I’m missing. I couldn’t find any real history of the car during a quick search, but Pete Lovely’s name is on the headrest, and he’s a known driver (he raced Lotuses in Formula 1). Plus, some deep research would (hopefully) be rewarding, and I can think of plenty of uses for this car, from vintage racing to just sitting in the garage and admiring it. Might have to shed a few pounds before fitting inside. — *Andrew Newton*


## Minty XK120


Gooding Christie's


Nice original color scheme[Jaguar XK120 OTS](https://www.goodingco.com/lot/1953-jaguar-xk120-se-roadster-pb26) . Sure, the 1997 registration sticker and missing air cleaners are a bit worrying, but it is a Jaguar and parts are available. Besides, I’m sure on some Porsche ordering form somewhere, ticking this box to get your new 911 in this color would be an additional $60K. — *John Wiley*


## Curved Dash Olds


Darin Schnabel/RM Sotheby's


The[1904 Curved Dash Oldsmobile](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/mo26/lots/s0001-1904-oldsmobile-model-6c-curveddash-runabout/) sold at RM Sotheby’s for $58,800 seems like a very nice example of an interesting early car (AACA Grand National first prize winner) that is potentially eligible for many events, including the London to Brighton Veteran Car Run. The price seems fair for the condition and is a rare find on this side of the Atlantic. — *John Mayhead*


## V-8 Wedge


Mecum


While the Quail was a-hoppin’ with new car reveals and[this 2001 Lotus Esprit](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1176391/2001-lotus-esprit/) was crossing the block in Monterey, I was making my way to Detroit for the Woodward Dream Cruise. That Saturday, while the avenue was packed mostly with American iron, a straight-piped Esprit V-8 rumbled past with the most lovely of exhaust notes. I’ve always loved these little Brit wedges. As a result, seeing this one on the list for $68K, well under our limit, got me thinking that I’d have plenty of budget left over to make it sound burbly as can be. — *Eddy Eckart*


## A Prancing 2+2


Mecum


The only thing I *don’t* like about[this Ferrari 456M GTA](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1176864/2001-ferrari-456m-gta/) is that it’s a conventional torque-converter automatic. Which, for the right price after the fact, can be swapped for a gated manual. Otherwise, this car represents a lot of what is wonderful and ineffable about Ferraris—beautiful, sophisticated, and anchored by a glorious V-12 engine up front. The light blue paint and cream interior scream coastal European luxury. For the $74,800 price, it’s a sensational GT car with modern creature comforts and even a couple of extra seats for luggage or kids, unlike the related two-seat Ferrari 550. Both automatic and 2+2 cars from Maranello suffer on the market compared with two-seaters and manuals, but whoever scored this car got a bargain, in my book. — *Eric Weiner*


## Old Hog, New Tricks?


Mecum


I’ve yet to ride a bike of this era, but some of the sporty models of the 1940s have always captured my interest. This ’42 Harley-Davidson WLD for $33,000 caught my eye because, aside from being low production, it also looks downright fun to ride and already matches the rest of the bikes in my garage. Probably against better judgment, I’d be inclined to return the foot-shift conversion to the original hand-shift for selecting one of the three gears in the transmission. Foot clutch, low bars, and a 45-cubic-inch flathead. Seems like a recipe for time travel. — *Kyle Smith*


## An ’80s Pairing


Bonhams


Mecum


How this sleek[shark of a German grand tourer](https://cars.bonhams.com/auction/31959/lot/37/1982-bmw-635csi-the-observer-coupe-vin-wbaec7209c8175000/#photos) is *less* than the Jeep is beyond me. Perhaps it’s a good thing that the pair would leave me with $30,000, because I can ensure that the BMW’s mechanicals are up to snuff and that any quirks of its one-off construction are addressed before taking it on a road trip Up North with my husband. The ’85 CJ-7 is the perfect weekend off-roader, and fresh off a pricey restoration. Both these choices are ’80s, though I love how the Jeep looks more vintage than its model year would suggest, and the BMW looks somehow more modern. Now, if only I had a garage to put these in! — *Grace Jarvis*


## C5 Hopes Spring Eternal


Mecum


I kind of suck at this game: I’m the sort of gambler who puts down $5 on red, and then, win or lose, walks away. And make no mistake—buying any vehicle at auction is a gamble. There’s a reason why every vehicle that crosses the block is for sale, and I can’t shake the assumption that the reason any vehicle I’d buy is for sale is that the engine and transmission are likely to just fall out onto the road the first time I shift into second gear. So, even playing with somebody else’s money, I’m going way conservative here. That said, I still love the C5/C6/C7 Chevrolet Corvettes, and I’m hoping that the reason[this 2003 Corvette Coupe](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1175747/2003-chevrolet-corvette-coupe/) with a manual transmission went for just $11,000 at Mecum’s auction is that it was a Thursday morning car and was presented to a not-yet-awake crowd of bidders. I like the color (Medium Spiral Gray outside, Light Oak inside), I like the powertrain, the wheels, the two tops; 86,000 miles? Seems about right. And at $11,000, if the engine and transmission do fall onto the ground, I’ll cry, but likely won’t sob… I’ll just ask our[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/) to stitch it all back together. — *Steven Cole Smith*


## Citroën DS 21 Dreaming


Broad Arrow


When I was eight, my dad had a DS Safari, so I’ve always had a thing for shark-nose Citroëns of a certain age. An SM has been living rent-free in my head for almost my whole life, but compared to this stunning Chapron coupe, the Maserati-motored machine is a mere baguette to a glorious gateau. Just 35 of these DS21s were rebodied by the Gallic genius Henri Chapron, and[this one, which sold for $95,200, was delivered new](https://www.broadarrowauctions.com/vehicles/ql26_r0085/1965-citroen-ds-21-chapron-concorde) to a French architect, who got to drive around in the equivalent of a rolling Pompidou Center. In my auction dreams, I’m doing that now. — *Nik Berg*


## Stefan’s Rollin’ a Highboy


Mecum


I think the last time we did this exercise I spent all my money on a BMW 3.0CSL, and I’m probably still very busy enjoying it. So despite Broad Arrow offering a gorgeous ’72 in an eye-popping yellow, I decided to pass on adding another to the collection and instead am going for some rugged, modern utility with the[1970 Ford F-250 Custom Highboy](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1175711/1970-ford-f-250-custom-highboy-pickup/) that Mecum sold for $89,100. The thought of old trucks at this price is hard to stomach, until you see what all has been done to this fully restored fella, with its Coyote V-8 and six-speed transmission, rebuilt Dana components, updated electrical system, on and on and on. All while looking exactly the way I’d want a 56-year-old ranch truck to look. And though I might miss the seat springs poking me in the butt through an old Mexican blanket, I’m sure I’d learn to live with the comfort of the new leather bench. — *Stefan Lombard*


## Nate finds a Z


Broad Arrow


I didn’t expect this to be my pick, but after the page loaded, I was gobsmacked by how handsome this 1971 Datsun 240Z was. Silver might typically be a boring color, but it works so, so well here. This thing has the perfect wheels on it already, and it was recently serviced so it should be set for many, many miles of cruising. This side profile shot is just stunning. Instead of a second car, I’d probably spend a good chunk of the remaining $49K setting up tours of this country’s greatest roads. Maybe I’d fork over some coin to get it track-ready as well, and go see if I can let that straight-six sing on a couple of straightaways, too. — *Nathan Petroelje*
